claim: Focal seizures have been recognized for more than 3000 years, with descriptions dating back to ancient Mesopotamia.
source: Focal seizures have been recognized for more than 3000 years, with descriptions dating back to ancient Mesopotamia (Worthington, 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to Worthington, 2005

claim: Focal seizures present with consistent clinical and large-scale EEG features including propagation from a focal onset location to large brain regions, widespread neuronal synchronization, a transition from tonic to clonic activity, and a slowing pace of neuronal discharging prior to simultaneous seizure termination.
source: Although focal seizures can present with a plethora of behavioral manifestations that vary according to the affected cortical regions, there are several consistent clinical and large-scale EEG features (Kotagal et al., 2008): propagation from a focal onset location to large brain regions, widespread neuronal synchronization, a transition from tonic to clonic activity, and a slowing pace of neuronal discharging prior to simultaneous seizure termination.
evidence: Supported by citation to Kotagal et al., 2008

claim: Microelectrode array recordings in humans identified neuronal underpinnings of common seizure features.
source: Our recent investigations, utilizing microelectrode array recordings in humans, identified neuronal underpinnings of these common seizure features (Schevon et al., 2012; Smith et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Schevon et al., 2012 and Smith et al., 2016

claim: Focal seizures have a dual spatial structure consisting of a core region of seizing brain bounded by an ictal wavefront surrounded by a passively reactive penumbra.
source: Based on these findings and results from animal model studies (Trevelyan et al., 2006; Trevelyan et al., 2007a; Trevelyan et al., 2007b; Wenzel et al., 2017; Wenzel et al., 2019), we proposed a dual spatial structure for focal seizures consisting of a core region of seizing brain bounded by an ictal wavefront surrounded by a passively reactive penumbra.
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies including Trevelyan et al., 2006, 2007a, 2007b, Wenzel et al., 2017, 2019

claim: The ictal wavefront is a narrow band of intense, desynchronized multiunit (tonic) firing that marks the transition to seizure at a given brain location.
source: What delineates the boundary of the ictal core is the ictal wavefront, a narrow band of intense, desynchronized multiunit (tonic) firing that marks the transition to seizure at a given brain location.
evidence: Direct statement in the manuscript describing the ictal wavefront

claim: Tonic firing structure of the ictal wavefront is typically not detectable in clinical EEG or band-limited local field potentials.
source: Typically, this tonic firing structure is not detectable in clinical EEG or band-limited local field potentials (LFPs).
evidence: Direct statement about detectability of tonic firing in EEG/LFP

claim: Collapse of inhibition is the key element causing ictal wavefront propagation, which leads to progressive seizure territory expansion.
source: Evidence from human (Schevon et al., 2012) and animal studies (Trevelyan et al., 2006; Trevelyan et al., 2007b) suggests that collapse of inhibition is the key element causing ictal wavefront propagation, which leads to progressive seizure territory expansion.
evidence: Supported by citations to human and animal studies

claim: The slow pace of ictal wavefront propagation (<1 mm/sec) corresponds to the slow evolution of the electrographic seizure and clinical semiology.
source: The slow pace of ictal wavefront propagation (<1 mm/sec) corresponds to the slow evolution of the electrographic seizure and clinical semiology, for example the classic Jacksonian march (York and Steinberg, 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to York and Steinberg, 2011

claim: The ictal wavefront generates fast-moving ictal discharges directed inward towards the initiation point at speeds two orders of magnitude higher than the wavefront propagation.
source: As it advances, the ictal wavefront generates fast-moving ictal discharges (Trevelyan, 2009; Smith et al., 2016), directed inward towards the initiation point, at speeds two orders of magnitude higher than the wavefront propagation (Smith et al., 2016; Liou et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Trevelyan, 2009; Smith et al., 2016; Liou et al., 2017

claim: Fast-moving ictal discharges are the basis of the well-recognized high amplitude field potential deflections that are the hallmark of electrographic seizures.
source: These fast-moving ictal discharges are the basis of the well-recognized high amplitude field potential deflections that are the hallmark of electrographic seizures.
evidence: Direct statement linking fast-moving discharges to EEG features

claim: There are two types of moving waves that characterize seizures: fast, inward-moving ictal discharges and the slow outward-moving wavefront of ictal recruitment.
source: Thus, there are two types of moving waves that characterize seizures: fast, inward-moving ictal discharges and the slow outward-moving wavefront of ictal recruitment.
evidence: Summary statement of the two wave types

claim: No prior theoretical study has shown how the dynamic topological structure of seizures can arise from basic biophysical mechanisms.
source: To date, despite extensive prior work in computational seizure modeling (Soltesz and Staley, 2011), no theoretical study has shown how this dynamic topological structure can arise from basic biophysical mechanisms.
evidence: Statement about gap in prior literature, with citation to Soltesz and Staley, 2011

claim: Phenomenological models like Epileptor have successfully utilized large-scale functional EEG features to reproduce the large-area, apparently synchronized EEG activity that characterizes clinical seizure recordings.
source: Phenomenological models, such as Epileptor (Jirsa et al., 2014; Proix et al., 2018), have successfully utilized large-scale functional EEG features to reproduce the large-area, apparently synchronized EEG activity that characterizes clinical seizure recordings, although identifying smaller scale neurophysiological processes corresponding to each abstract variable in these models can be challenging.
evidence: Supported by citations to Jirsa et al., 2014 and Proix et al., 2018

claim: Biophysical models have been used to explore the role of specific neurophysiological processes responsible for seizure transitions, such as intracellular and extracellular potassium dynamics.
source: Biophysical models have been used to explore the role of specific neurophysiological processes responsible for seizure transitions, such as intracellular and extracellular potassium dynamics (Cressman et al., 2009; Ullah et al., 2009), transmembrane chloride gradients (Buchin et al., 2016), and calcium-activated processes (Yang et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citations to Cressman et al., 2009 and Ullah et al., 2009

claim: The evolving, wide-area dynamics that characterize the life cycle of a seizure remain difficult to explain by any single biophysical mechanism.
source: However, the evolving, wide-area dynamics that characterize the life cycle of a seizure remain difficult to explain by any single biophysical mechanism.
evidence: Statement about limitations of current biophysical models

claim: The model neocortex is represented as a 2-dimensional neuron sheet.
source: We modeled the neocortex as a 2-dimensional neuron sheet (Bressloff, 2014).
evidence: Direct statement about model structure, with citation to Bressloff, 2014

claim: Model neurons are pyramidal cell-like and contain two intrinsic conductances (leak and slow potassium) and two synaptic conductances (excitatory AMPA and inhibitory GABA-A).
source: Model neurons are pyramidal cell-like and contain two intrinsic conductances – leak and slow potassium – and two synaptic conductances – excitatory (AMPA) and inhibitory (GABA-A).
evidence: Direct description of model neuron properties

claim: Model neurons incorporate spike-frequency adaptation mechanisms through neuronal firing increasing the spike threshold and activating an additional slow afterhyperpolarization (sAHP) conductance.
source: Model neurons incorporate spike-frequency adaptation mechanisms – neuronal firing increases the spike threshold and activates an additional slow afterhyperpolarization (sAHP) conductance.
evidence: Direct description of adaptation mechanisms in the model

claim: The range of di-synaptic recurrent inhibition is longer than the mono-synaptic excitatory range, creating a 'Mexican hat' structure of effective synaptic weights.
source: The effects of recurrent projections between model neurons are hypothesized to be distance-dependent, with the range of di-synaptic recurrent inhibition longer than the mono-synaptic excitatory range, thereby making the spatial distribution of the effective synaptic weights from a model neuron follows a 'Mexican hat' structure (Prince and Wilder, 1967; Coombes, 2005; Bressloff, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Prince and Wilder, 1967; Coombes, 2005; Bressloff, 2014

claim: The model includes a distance-independent recurrent inhibition pathway inspired by recent observation of large-scale inhibitory effects of focal seizure activity.
source: In addition, our model includes a distance-independent recurrent inhibition pathway (Figure 1A, part γ), inspired by recent observation of large-scale inhibitory effects of focal seizure activity (Eissa et al., 2017; Liou et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Eissa et al., 2017 and Liou et al., 2018

claim: In its original form, the model does not spontaneously seize and model seizures are initiated by transient focal excitatory inputs.
source: In its original form, the model does not spontaneously seize. Instead model seizures are initiated by transient focal excitatory inputs.
evidence: Direct statement about model behavior

claim: The model can be considered a model of a healthy neural circuit, with the degree of resistance to seizure controlled by its parameters.
source: This model can be considered a model of a healthy neural circuit, with the degree of resistance to seizure controlled by its parameters.
evidence: Direct statement about model interpretation

claim: Patient A's microelectrode array recording demonstrates a slow, progressive advancement of seizing neuronal activity from the left to right side of the array-sampled area.
source: The human recording demonstrates a slow, progressive advancement of seizing neuronal activity from the left to right side of the array-sampled area (Figure 1B, left, orange arrows).
evidence: Observation from patient data shown in Figure 1B

claim: Following the brief period of tonic firing marking the passage of the ictal wavefront, neurons inside the ictal core transition to repetitive bursting.
source: Following the brief period of tonic firing marking the passage of the ictal wavefront, the neurons, now inside the ictal core, transitioned to repetitive bursting (Figure 1B, right).
evidence: Observation from patient data shown in Figure 1B

claim: Bursts propagate sequentially in space from the ictal wavefront back toward the internal domain, constituting fast-moving 'inward traveling waves'.
source: Bursts propagated sequentially in space from the ictal wavefront back toward the internal domain, constituting fast-moving 'inward traveling waves' (Figure 1B, right, the blue arrow).
evidence: Observation from patient data shown in Figure 1B

claim: The model reproduces key dynamics seen in human recordings, including the slow-marching wavefront and the subsequent fast inward traveling waves.
source: The key dynamics seen in the human recordings were reproduced by the model, including the slow-marching wavefront (Figure 1C, right, orange arrows) and the subsequent fast inward traveling waves (Figure 1C, right, the blue arrow).
evidence: Comparison between model output (Figure 1C) and patient data

claim: A transient excitatory input triggers the establishment of a localized, self-sustaining tonic firing region near the bottom of the space, marking the onset of the model seizure.
source: In this model, a transient excitatory input triggers the establishment of a localized, self-sustaining tonic firing region near the bottom of the space, marking the onset of the model seizure (Figure 2A, green diamond).
evidence: Description of model behavior shown in Figure 2A

claim: The seizure territory initially expands bidirectionally until all neurons near the bottom of the space are recruited, at which point it can only expand towards the top.
source: The seizure territory initially expands bidirectionally until all neurons near the bottom of the space are recruited, at which point it can only expand towards the top.
evidence: Description of model dynamics

claim: The 'activity bump' eventually collapses and transitions spontaneously into repetitive neuronal bursting, marking the transition from the ictal-tonic to the ictal-clonic stage.
source: The 'activity bump' eventually collapses and transitions spontaneously into repetitive neuronal bursting, marking the transition from the ictal-tonic to the ictal-clonic stage (Figure 2A, green star).
evidence: Description of model behavior shown in Figure 2A

claim: Fast inward waves travel two orders of magnitude faster than the slowly expanding ictal wavefront, with a ratio of 170.
source: In comparison to the slowly expanding ictal wavefront, the fast inward waves travel two orders of magnitude faster (Figure 2B, ratio = 170).
evidence: Quantitative measurement from model shown in Figure 2B

claim: The ratio of fast inward wave speed to ictal wavefront speed in the model approximates that previously reported in human recordings (average speed 0.83±0.14 mm/sec for ictal wavefront expansion versus post-recruitment ictal discharge traveling speeds of 26±24 cm/sec).
source: This ratio approximates that previously reported in human recordings, that is average speed 0.83±0.14 mm/sec for ictal wavefront expansion (Schevon et al., 2012) versus post-recruitment ictal discharge traveling speeds of 26±24 cm/sec (mean±s.d.) (Smith et al., 2016; Liou et al., 2017).
evidence: Comparison to human data with citations to Schevon et al., 2012; Smith et al., 2016; Liou et al., 2017

claim: As the seizure nears termination, the ictal wavefront dissipates, marking the beginning of the pre-termination stage.
source: As the seizure nears termination, the ictal wavefront dissipates (Figure 2A, green solid arrow), marking the beginning of the pre-termination stage.
evidence: Description of model behavior shown in Figure 2A

claim: After the last burst propagates across modeled brain region, the seizure terminates abruptly.
source: After the last burst propagates across modeled brain region, the seizure terminates abruptly (Figure 2A, green triangle).
evidence: Description of model behavior shown in Figure 2A

claim: The key dynamics of each seizure stage are corroborated and validated in the corresponding 1-dimensional integrate-and-fire spiking model that includes threshold noise.
source: The key dynamics of each of these seizure stages are further corroborated and validated in the corresponding 1-dimensional integrate-and-fire spiking model (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), that includes threshold noise.
evidence: Reference to validation in spiking model shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1

claim: The sequence of seizure stages is not affected by duration, spatial extent, or intensity of the external seizure-provoking inputs as long as they are adequate to trigger seizure onsets.
source: The sequence of seizure stages is not affected by duration, spatial extent, or intensity of the external seizure-provoking inputs as long as they are adequate to trigger seizure onsets (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Description of model behavior shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2

claim: Inputs that are inadequate to initiate a seizure, yet are near enough to the threshold for seizure induction, may trigger short-runs of 'after-discharges'.
source: Inputs that are inadequate to initiate a seizure, yet are near enough to the threshold for seizure induction, may trigger short-runs of 'after-discharges' (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: Description of model behavior shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A

claim: The slow propagation of the modelled ictal wavefront results from two sequentially activated processes: usage-dependent exhaustion of inhibition and upregulation of adaptation currents.
source: The slow propagation of the modelled ictal wavefront results from two sequentially activated processes: usage-dependent exhaustion of inhibition and upregulation of adaptation currents (Figure 2C).
evidence: Description of model mechanisms shown in Figure 2C

claim: Usage-dependent exhaustion of inhibition and upregulation of adaptation currents are modeled as intracellular chloride accumulation and sAHP conductance activation, respectively.
source: These are modeled as intracellular chloride accumulation and sAHP conductance activation, respectively.
evidence: Direct statement about model implementation

claim: As the ictal wavefront approaches, intracellular chloride starts to accumulate just ahead of it due to strong feedforward inhibition projected from the ictal core.
source: As the ictal wavefront approaches (Figure 2B, red bracket and Figure 2C, black arrow), intracellular chloride starts to accumulate just ahead of it (brown arrow) due to strong feedforward inhibition projected from the ictal core.
evidence: Description of model mechanism shown in Figures 2B and 2C

claim: Intracellular chloride accumulation causes the chloride reversal potential to become less negative, which compromises the strength of GABA-A receptor-mediated inhibition.
source: Intracellular chloride accumulation causes the chloride reversal potential to become less negative, which compromises the strength of GABA-A receptor-mediated inhibition (Materials and methods, Equation 3).
evidence: Description of model mechanism with reference to equation

claim: As the chloride reversal potential becomes less negative, inhibition is eventually overcome, causing neurons to transition from the resting to the tonic-firing state as they join the ictal wavefront.
source: As the chloride reversal potential becomes less negative, inhibition is eventually overcome, causing neurons to transition from the resting to the tonic-firing state as they join the ictal wavefront.
evidence: Description of model mechanism

claim: Intense neuronal firing activates the sAHP conductance, which mediates a hyperpolarizing potassium current that curbs neuronal excitability.
source: Intense neuronal firing subsequently activates the sAHP conductance (Figure 2C, blue arrow) (Materials and methods, Equation 4), which mediates a hyperpolarizing potassium current that curbs neuronal excitability.
evidence: Description of model mechanism shown in Figure 2C with reference to equation

claim: The tonically firing neurons in the ictal wavefront transition into repetitive bursts alternating with periods of silence, forming the periodic inward traveling waves.
source: Consequently, the tonically firing neurons in the ictal wavefront transition into repetitive bursts alternating with periods of silence, forming the periodic inward traveling waves described above.
evidence: Description of model behavior

claim: The sequence of intracellular chloride accumulation followed by the activation of sAHP mediates both the slow propagation of the ictal wavefront and the periodic, inward fast traveling waves that characterize the ictal core.
source: The sequence of intracellular chloride accumulation followed by the activation of sAHP thus mediates both the slow propagation of the ictal wavefront and the periodic, inward fast traveling waves that characterize the ictal core.
evidence: Summary statement of model mechanisms

claim: Model cortices in which neurons can pump out chloride quickly are resistant to seizure invasion.
source: Model cortices in which neurons can pump out chloride quickly are resistant to seizure invasion.
evidence: Description of model behavior

claim: If chloride can be pumped out fast enough (τCl≤ 3 sec), the model is unable to form self-sustaining seizures.
source: Ultimately, if chloride can be pumped out fast enough, the model is unable to form self-sustaining seizures (Figure 2D, τCl≤ 3 sec).
evidence: Description of model behavior shown in Figure 2D

claim: Increasing the sAHP conductance results in earlier tonic-clonic transitions, earlier seizure termination, and therefore a smaller seizure territory.
source: As shown in Figure 2E, increasing the sAHP conductance results in earlier tonic-clonic transitions, earlier seizure termination, and therefore a smaller seizure territory.
evidence: Description of model behavior shown in Figure 2E

claim: For high levels of the sAHP conductance (ΔK ≥ 0.25 nS/Hz), seizure initiation fails.
source: For high levels of the sAHP conductance, seizure initiation fails (Figure 2E, ΔK ≥ 0.25 nS/Hz).
evidence: Description of model behavior shown in Figure 2E

claim: In a parameter regime with robust inhibition and strong adaptation, the ictal core cannot be established, making the models resistant to the seizure-provoking insults.
source: In a parameter regime with robust inhibition and strong adaptation, the ictal core cannot be established, making the models resistant to the seizure-provoking insults.
evidence: Summary of model behavior

claim: Dissipation of the ictal wavefront is a key event preceding wide-area, simultaneous seizure termination.
source: Previously, based on analysis of human multiscale recordings, our group proposed that dissipation of the ictal wavefront is a key event preceding wide-area, simultaneous seizure termination (Smith et al., 2016; Liou et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Smith et al., 2016 and Liou et al., 2017

claim: As the seizure territory expands, the ictal wavefront in the model encounters increasingly stronger inhibition ahead of itself due to non-localized recurrent inhibition becoming progressively activated.
source: As the seizure territory expands, the ictal wavefront in the model encounters increasingly stronger inhibition ahead of itself. Such stronger inhibition is a result of non-localized recurrent inhibition (the global part of Equation 5 in Materials and methods) becoming progressively activated as more cortical areas are recruited into the seizing territory.
evidence: Description of model mechanism

claim: The dynamics function as a spatial integrator, with strength of inhibition proportional to the extent of the area that has been invaded.
source: The dynamics thus function as a spatial integrator, with strength of inhibition proportional to the extent of the area that has been invaded.
evidence: Description of model mechanism

claim: Seizure propagation gradually slows as the wavefront expands.
source: Consequentially, seizure propagation gradually slows as the wavefront expands.
evidence: Description of model behavior

claim: Once the propagation speed is inadequate to escape from sAHP-induced suppression, the wavefront is annihilated, and the seizure transitions into the pre-termination stage.
source: Once the propagation speed is inadequate to escape from sAHP-induced suppression, the wavefront is annihilated, and the seizure transitions into the pre-termination stage (Figure 2A green arrow and Figure 3).
evidence: Description of model behavior shown in Figures 2A and 3

claim: The pre-termination stage of a model seizure shows four characteristic trends: decreasing peak firing rate, increasing inter-burst intervals, decreasing inward traveling wave speed, and increasing burst width.
source: The pre-termination stage of a model seizure (Figure 3A) shows four characteristic trends: decreasing peak firing rate, increasing inter-burst intervals, decreasing inward traveling wave speed, and increasing burst width (Figure 3B).
evidence: Description of model behavior shown in Figures 3A and 3B

claim: These 'slowing-down' trends in the model match clinical observations as well as microelectrode recordings from epilepsy patients.
source: These 'slowing-down' trends match clinical observations as well as microelectrode recordings from epilepsy patients (Figure 3C–F, Source data 2; Source data 3; Source data 4).
evidence: Comparison between model and patient data shown in Figures 3C-F

claim: Increased duration of the silent period following each burst allows more time for recovery of inhibition strength, as more chloride can be removed from the intracellular space to restore the transmembrane chloride gradient.
source: Increased duration of the silent period following each burst (Figure 3D) allows more time for recovery of inhibition strength, as more chloride can be removed from the intracellular space to restore the transmembrane chloride gradient.
evidence: Description of model mechanism with reference to Figure 3D

claim: Recovered inhibition attenuates burst intensity, slows the speed of the inward traveling waves, and desynchronizes the neuronal population.
source: Recovered inhibition then attenuates burst intensity (Figure 3C), slows the speed of the inward traveling waves (Figure 3E), and desynchronizes the neuronal population (Figure 3F).
evidence: Description of model behavior shown in Figures 3C, 3E, and 3F

claim: Any mechanism that compromises inhibition strength, operates over a time scale of seconds and is triggered by intense inhibition usage is a possible candidate mechanism for the slow expansion of both the seizure territory and the pre-termination dynamics.
source: We hypothesized that any mechanism that compromises inhibition strength, operates over a time scale of seconds and is triggered by intense inhibition usage is a possible candidate mechanism for the slow expansion of both the seizure territory and the pre-termination dynamics.
evidence: Statement of hypothesis

claim: All evolutionary stages of focal seizures and their characteristic dynamics were reproduced using a generic inhibition exhaustion process instead of the chloride accumulation assumption.
source: To confirm our hypothesis, we modeled a generalized inhibition exhaustion process instead of using the chloride accumulation assumption (Materials and methods, Equation 8). All evolutionary stages of focal seizures and their characteristic dynamics were reproduced using this generic process (Figure 2—figure supplement 4).
evidence: Description of model behavior shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4

claim: When recurrent projections favor strong localized inhibition, seizure onset is characterized by a localized tonic-firing area, resulting in focal LVFA.
source: When recurrent projections favor strong localized inhibition, seizure onset is characterized by a localized tonic-firing area, resulting in focal LVFA (Figure 4A, 5:1 ratio of local versus global recurrent inhibition, Materials and methods, Equation 5).
evidence: Description of model behavior shown in Figure 4A

claim: The onset pattern shifts to rhythmic discharges when the distribution of recurrent inhibition favors spatially non-specific projections.
source: The onset pattern shifts to rhythmic discharges when the distribution of recurrent inhibition favors spatially non-specific projections (Figure 4B, 1:1 ratio of local versus global recurrent inhibition, Materials and methods, Equation 5).
evidence: Description of model behavior shown in Figure 4B

claim: Under conditions favoring spatially non-specific inhibition, inadequate local inhibitory restraint allows ictogenic perturbations to spread quickly outward in the form of traveling waves, generating rhythmic discharges as typically observed in the LFP bands.
source: Under this latter condition, inadequate local inhibitory restraint allows ictogenic perturbations to spread quickly outward in the form of traveling waves, generating rhythmic discharges as typically observed in the LFP bands.
evidence: Description of model mechanism

claim: The model predicts that various LFP patterns may coexist during a single seizure episode, depending on regional variances in the distribution of recurrent connectivity.
source: Our model further predicts that various LFP patterns may coexist during a single seizure episode, depending on regional variances in the distribution of recurrent connectivity (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Model prediction shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1

claim: The model predicts that outward traveling waves move at a lower speed than inward traveling waves because inhibition outside the ictal wavefront is initially intact.
source: Also, our model predicts that outward traveling waves move at a lower speed than inward traveling waves because inhibition outside the ictal wavefront is initially intact (Figure 4B).
evidence: Model prediction shown in Figure 4B

claim: A similar dependence of traveling wave speed on the direction relative to the ictal wavefront has been observed in human recordings.
source: In agreement with our prediction, as shown in Figure 4C, a similar dependence of traveling wave speed on the direction relative to the ictal wavefront has been observed in human recordings (Source data 2; Source data 3; Source data 4; Smith et al., 2016; Liou et al., 2017).
evidence: Comparison to human data shown in Figure 4C with citations

claim: During a provoked seizure, inward traveling waves selectively enhanced excitatory projections from the periphery to the internal domain of the ictal core due to pre-before-post potentiation in STDP.
source: During a provoked seizure (Figure 5A), inward traveling waves, because of pre-before-post potentiation in STDP, selectively enhanced excitatory projections from the periphery to the internal domain of the ictal core, in accordance with the predominant traveling wave direction (Figure 5B, left).
evidence: Description of model behavior shown in Figures 5A and 5B

claim: The newly created spatial bias of excitatory projections follows a centripetal pattern.
source: This newly created spatial bias of excitatory projections therefore follows a centripetal pattern (Figure 5B, right, see Materials and methods, section Spike-Timing Dependent Plasticity for quantification of spatial biases of synaptic projections).
evidence: Description of model behavior shown in Figure 5B

claim: Strengthening of centripetal connectivity can predispose the neural network to more seizures by funneling background neural activity into its center.
source: Such strengthening of centripetal connectivity can predispose the neural network to more seizures by funneling background neural activity into its center.
evidence: Description of model mechanism

claim: A background input which is non-ictogenic in a naïve network may provoke seizures in the remodeled network by evoking centripetal traveling waves, which can exhaust inhibition strength at the center of the increased centripetal connectivity.
source: Furthermore, as shown in Figure 5C, a background input which is non-ictogenic in a naïve network may now provoke seizures in the remodeled network by evoking centripetal traveling waves, which can exhaust inhibition strength at the center of the increased centripetal connectivity.
evidence: Description of model behavior shown in Figure 5C

claim: Subsequent seizures are prone to be triggered from the same location, and their associated inward traveling waves can further reciprocally strengthen the centripetal connectivity.
source: Subsequent seizures are therefore prone to be triggered from the same location, and their associated inward traveling waves can further reciprocally strengthen this centripetal connectivity.
evidence: Description of model mechanism

claim: The model predicts that epileptiform discharges preceding LVFA seizure onset travel toward the seizure center, rather than away from it.
source: Results from seizures generated by our model after the network remodeling described above predict that epileptiform discharges preceding LVFA seizure onset travel toward the seizure center, rather than away from it (Figure 5C).
evidence: Model prediction shown in Figure 5C

claim: Centripetal traveling waves have been observed in the microelectrode recordings of spontaneous human seizures immediately before the onset of an LVFA seizure.
source: Such centripetal traveling waves have been observed in the microelectrode recordings of spontaneous human seizures (Source data 1) immediately before the onset of an LVFA seizure (Figure 5D–F, compared to Figure 1B).
evidence: Observation from patient data shown in Figures 5D-F

claim: Large-amplitude epileptiform discharges with associated multiunit bursts were present just prior to seizure onset in Patient A, spreading from right to left, which is the same direction as the rapidly traveling inward waves of ictal discharges, and opposite to the direction of seizure expansion.
source: In particular, large-amplitude epileptiform discharges with associated multiunit bursts were present just prior to seizure onset, spreading from right to left (Figure 5E–F). This is the same direction as the rapidly traveling inward waves of ictal discharges, and opposite to the direction of seizure expansion (Figure 1B).
evidence: Observation from patient data shown in Figures 5E-F and 1B

claim: Under noise-free conditions, a seizure evoked at the center of the neural sheet expands with a perfectly circular ictal wavefront.
source: Under the noise-free condition considered up to this point, a seizure evoked at the center of the neural sheet expands with a perfectly circular ictal wavefront (Figure 6A and Figure 6—video 1).
evidence: Description of model behavior shown in Figure 6A

claim: In the noise-free case, all inward traveling waves are directed in a centripetal pattern uniformly towards the center point, with no directional preference within the ictal core.
source: All inward traveling waves in this case are directed in a centripetal pattern uniformly towards the center point, with no directional preference within the ictal core (Figure 6A and Figure 6—video 1).
evidence: Description of model behavior shown in Figure 6A

claim: Ictal EEG discharges recorded from epilepsy patients demonstrate stable preferred traveling wave directions.
source: However, ictal EEG discharges recorded from epilepsy patients clearly demonstrate stable preferred traveling wave directions (Smith et al., 2016; Liou et al., 2017; Martinet et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Smith et al., 2016; Liou et al., 2017; Martinet et al., 2017

claim: Traveling wave direction bias may occur due to random fluctuations in background neural activity even in a round, symmetric environment.
source: Although preferred directions can arise from pre-existing spatial asymmetry (Figure 1—video 1), our simulation of a seizure occurring at the round, symmetric environment indicates that the traveling wave direction bias may also occur due to random fluctuations in background neural activity (Figure 6—video 2).
evidence: Description of model behavior shown in Figure 6—video 2

claim: Uniformly distributed, spatiotemporally white noise can create a long-lasting, preferred inward traveling wave direction without any requirement for spatial asymmetry or inhomogeneity of the neural sheet.
source: Instead, our model shows that uniformly distributed, spatiotemporally white noise can create a long-lasting, preferred inward traveling wave direction without any requirement for spatial asymmetry or inhomogeneity of the neural sheet (Figure 6B, also see Figure 6—video 2).
evidence: Description of model behavior shown in Figure 6B

claim: After the tonic-to-clonic transition in the model, background noise first randomly creates a bias of the confluence point where the inward traveling waves meet.
source: After the tonic-to-clonic transition in the model, background noise first randomly creates a bias of the confluence point where the inward traveling waves meet (Figure 6C).
evidence: Description of model behavior shown in Figure 6C

claim: Once established, the bias persists and, due to the low pass property of the neural sheet, it can only slowly drift, resulting in a sustained traveling wave direction preference lasting until the pre-termination stage.
source: Once established, the bias persists and, due to the low pass property of the neural sheet, it can only slowly drift, resulting in a sustained traveling wave direction preference lasting until the pre-termination stage.
evidence: Description of model mechanism

claim: After wavefront annihilation, traveling wave directions randomly fluctuate and flip.
source: After wavefront annihilation, traveling wave directions randomly fluctuate and flip (Figure 6D).
evidence: Description of model behavior shown in Figure 6D

claim: Variable wave directions after wavefront annihilation mimic human seizure recordings, where an increase in the variability of wave directions and 'flip-flop' direction reversals are present before seizure termination.
source: Such variable wave directions mimic human seizure recordings, where an increase in the variability of wave directions and 'flip-flop' direction reversals are present before seizure termination (Figure 6—figure supplement 1; Trevelyan et al., 2007a).
evidence: Comparison to human data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1 with citation to Trevelyan et al., 2007a

claim: Three out of ten repeated simulations under background current noise showed failure of spontaneous seizure termination.
source: We repeated the simulation shown in Figure 6B under the same level of background current noise. Three out of ten repeated simulations showed failure of spontaneous seizure termination.
evidence: Quantitative result from model simulations

claim: The persistent seizure scenario is characterized by the formation of spiral waves that emerge after wavefront annihilation and exhibit complex interactions.
source: The persistent seizure scenario is characterized by the formation of spiral waves that emerge after wavefront annihilation (Figure 7A) and exhibit complex interactions (Figure 7B).
evidence: Description of model behavior shown in Figures 7A and 7B

claim: In one simulation example, one spiral wave eventually dominated the space, self-attracted, and persisted indefinitely, resulting in model status epilepticus.
source: In the example shown, one spiral wave eventually dominated the space, self-attracted, and persisted indefinitely, resulting in model status epilepticus (Figure 7B and Figure 7—video 1).
evidence: Description of model behavior shown in Figure 7B

claim: The coexistence of endpoints corresponding to spontaneous seizure termination or status epilepticus under background current noise suggests bistable dynamics of seizure evolution.
